This paper describes how the Bayesian approach to statistical data analysis can be used for the calibration of groups of radiocarbon results in situations where archaeological information is available *a priori* about the relationships between the contexts being dated. Recent innovations in the implementation of the Bayesian paradigm are used and the methodology is illustrated by the analysis of data arising from two archaeological excavations. * C.E. Buck *et al.*. ### Combining archaeological and radiocarbon information: a Bayesian approach to calibration. ### Some statistical problems arising in radiocarbon calibration. The one that is employed in this paper is the Bayesian approach which allows us to combine information of a probabilistic nature in a formal way and which has been applied in various forms in palaeo-climate records recently (e.g. see Walker et al., 2003; Blockley et al., 2004). Bayesian methods have been applied to constrained radiocarbon dates for many years now (Buck et al., 1991, 1992) and with greater frequency since the availability of software to perform such analyses (Bronk Ramsey, 1995, 2001; Jones and Nicholls, 2002). For details of Bayesian theory readers should look elsewhere (e.g. see Gilks et al., 1996; D’Agostini, 2003 and particularly Buck et al., 1996; Buck and Millard, 2001). Given the imprecision of individual calibrated radiocarbon determinations it is necessary to use the information we have about the deposition process to refine our chronologies and also to provide interpolation between dated levels in any sequence. This paper outlines a range of Bayesian models for deposition which have been implemented in the computer programme OxCal. These models can be used to combine information from the sediments themselves with radiocarbon or other direct dating information. Such models have the potential to integrate information between different records and provide a coherent chronology on which to base environmental or archaeological research. * ### Bayesian analysis of radiocarbon dates.

results.title: Essential Dating Methods in Archaeology to Know for Archaeology and Museums
results.content: # Essential Dating Methods in Archaeology. Dating methods aren't just technical procedures—they're the foundation of how archaeologists construct narratives about the past, and those narratives directly shape how museums present human history and cultural identity. When you're studying the politics of archaeology, you need to understand that **the choice of dating method can determine which stories get told** and which cultures get positioned as "ancient" or "developed." These techniques establish *chronological authority*, and that authority has real consequences for heritage claims, repatriation debates, and national identity construction. Exam questions will ask you to evaluate how dating methods support or challenge archaeological interpretations, how they've been used (and misused) to construct cultural narratives, and why certain methods carry more scientific credibility than others. *The key principle is that unstable atoms transform into stable ones at known rates, giving us a "clock" embedded in materials.* Absolute dating revolutionized archaeology by replacing subjective interpretation with measurable data—but remember, "absolute" doesn't mean "certain.". * **Dates volcanic rock and ash** by measuring potassium-40 decay to argon-40—effective for materials over 100,000 years old. Potassium-Argon—both measure radioactive decay, but radiocarbon dates organic materials in recent prehistory while K-Ar dates geological events in deep time. If an FRQ asks about dating early human evolution, K-Ar is your method; for Neolithic settlements, reach for radiocarbon. OSL—both measure trapped electrons, but TL requires heating events (human activity) while OSL dates light exposure (natural burial). *The underlying principle is that observable patterns—whether in soil layers or artifact styles—reflect temporal order.* Relative dating remains foundational even in an age of absolute methods. * **Provides exact calendar-year dates** by matching ring patterns in wood to established regional chronologies—precision unmatched by any other method. * **Serves as calibration standard** for radiocarbon dating, correcting for atmospheric carbon variations and anchoring other methods to real calendar time. * **Dates the last firing event**, useful for understanding site use history and activity sequences in contexts with repeated heating.
